name: Valproate
summary: A broad-spectrum anticonvulsant and mood stabilizer that is first-line for generalized (absence, myoclonic) epilepsies but carries major hepatotoxicity and teratogenicity risks.
mechanism: Enhances GABAergic transmission and blocks voltage-gated sodium channels; at higher doses inhibits histone deacetylase.

pharmacokinetics.proteinBinding: 85–90% (concentration-dependent; free fraction rises at high doses)

dosing.adult: Start 250–500 mg BID (divalproex); usual maintenance 1000–2000 mg/day divided

safety.pregnancy: Contraindicated — major teratogen (neural tube defects, reduced IQ, fetal valproate syndrome); avoid in women of childbearing age
contraindications: Hepatic disease or significant hepatic dysfunction
warnings: Hepatotoxicity — fatal hepatic failure, highest risk in children <2 years and with polytherapy
Teratogenicity (black-box warning) — neural tube defects and reduced IQ; avoid in women of childbearing age
Pancreatitis — can be fatal; stop drug if abdominal pain with nausea/vomiting
Hyperammonemic encephalopathy — especially with topiramate or urea cycle defects
Thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy at higher doses
safety.overdose: CNS depression, coma, cerebral edema, hyperammonemia; L-carnitine and hemodialysis in severe cases

clinicalPearls: First-line for idiopathic generalized epilepsies (absence, myoclonic) — but avoid in women of childbearing age
Free fraction rises at high doses (saturable protein binding) — monitor free levels when albumin is low
good: Idiopathic generalized epilepsy (absence, myoclonic) where it remains class-leading.
bad: Women of childbearing age, liver disease, or anyone on topiramate (hyperammonemia risk).
